title: Last House on the Block
subtitle: Mini-demo GDD & demand-validation roadmap
status: Proposed design—not a playable build, approved production budget or validated market gap. Working title is not cleared.
pitch: Scavenge the neighbourhood. The shortcut you open for yourself becomes the way they reach your home.
decision: Build a 10–15-minute solo first-person slice around one persistent route decision. The open-world ambition is a connected neighbourhood later; this sprint tests whether target players want this concentrated experience.
audience: Players who enjoy vulnerable, grounded survival and returning to an improved home. Recruit from people who actually play Project Zomboid, VEIN and 7 Days to Die, then record whether they mainly play solo or co-op.
nonAudience: Not yet for players buying vast maps, multiplayer servers, realistic firearms or complex construction. Do not recruit only friends who like the team, or advertise this as an alternative with every feature of those games.

hypotheses.name: Product
hypotheses.claim: A route that helps scavenging but increases night danger creates an understandable, personally owned survival story.
hypotheses.test: Observe the first choice, ask for an unprompted explanation after the night, then offer an optional second run.
hypotheses.failure: Players attribute the consequence to an arbitrary script or cannot identify a meaningful alternative.

hypotheses.name: Demand
hypotheses.claim: A specific subset of grounded-survival players wants this concentrated choice, even without a large map or co-op in the demo.
hypotheses.test: Recruit target players outside the team’s social circle and separate solo-first from co-op-first responses.
hypotheses.failure: Interest disappears when the actual solo scope is revealed, or feedback only requests a larger existing competitor.

hypotheses.name: Communication
hypotheses.claim: Real footage can explain the benefit and later cost of the same shortcut in 15 seconds.
hypotheses.test: Compare two openings made from the same build; ask what viewers think they would do, not just whether the clip is funny.
hypotheses.failure: The joke attracts reactions but viewers cannot describe a playable decision.

evidence.finding: The camera angle is not an empty niche: VEIN already advertises first-person zombie-survival systems.
evidence.implication: Differentiate the decision and feedback loop; do not pitch only 'Project Zomboid but FPS'.

evidence.finding: 7 Days to Die already offers a broad scavenging, building and zombie-defence package.
evidence.implication: Compete on a concentrated experience in the demo, not on the number of systems.

evidence.finding: HTMAG’s 2025 OWSC table is a historical review-threshold cohort, with tag-based supply approximation.
evidence.implication: It justifies investigating the audience, not forecasting a 20.8% chance of success.

evidence.finding: The trailer cases distinguish showing an action from explaining its purpose; the Inkbound postmortem exposes solo/co-op scope trade-offs.
evidence.implication: Prove one action-to-consequence chain and choose one supported play mode.

pillars.name: An ordinary home worth returning to
pillars.rule: The player begins in a visibly insecure refuge. Each useful pickup changes a specific problem at home.
pillars.proof: The same barricade is damaged at the start, repaired by the player and tested at night.

pillars.name: Convenience leaves a trace
pillars.rule: The route change persists and affects the enemy’s actual path, not just an invisible difficulty modifier.
pillars.proof: The infected visibly use the fence gap the player opened earlier.

pillars.name: Fair, readable regret
pillars.rule: The safe route remains viable. Give visual and audio warnings before a shortcut becomes dangerous.
pillars.proof: A cold player can explain both the saved effort and the new risk without a tooltip revealing the entire outcome.

scope.boundary: Use the engine and controller stack the two senior developers already ship with. No engine migration.
One safehouse, one two-room scavenging interior, two outdoor paths and a fenced shortcut. Dimensions are a starting layout target, not an optimized balance claim.

Target two supply runs in a 10–15-minute session, then an optional replay with another route choice. A prepared player may begin night after the first repair; two trips are a useful pattern, not an artificial mandatory gate.
Open or leave the fence shut. The same flag changes the player's route and the infected's route.

scope.item: Four inventory slots; three resource families
scope.boundary: Each slot holds one non-stacking resource unit. Melee tool is separate equipment. Two barricade upgrades each cost 3 scrap; one bandage costs 1 cloth. Place 8 scrap, 3 cloth and 2 food across the fixed map as initial tuning values; test, do not treat them as proven balance.

scope.item: One infected archetype, maximum six active
scope.boundary: A small state machine and baked navigation with switchable links. One melee tool; fleeing and blocking are viable.

Healthy capacity is four; wounded capacity is three. If the affected slot is occupied, move its item to a free slot or visibly drop it at a reachable fixed pickup anchor, preserving its identity. One cloth cures the wound; no loss of an essential item.
Keep route, loot, inventory, wound and barricade state through both trips. No world simulation while off-screen.
Do not expand the navigation/state matrix after day seven. Consider this only in the next experiment, after the fence-only demo and release candidate are stable.
The earlier concept offered these as possibilities; this GDD removes them from the baseline to protect the route-choice loop.

scope.item: Full open world, multiplayer, procedural terrain and freeform building
scope.boundary: Also cut vehicles, NPC survivors, seasons, nutrition simulation, structural destruction, crafting trees and a weapon catalogue.

playthrough.player: See a weak barricade and a simple supply goal. Walk, look, interact and inspect four slots.
playthrough.system: Start with a clear silhouette and nearby material example. Do not begin with lore exposition.

playthrough.player: Choose the longer route or open the fence. Carry scrap back through the route you chose.
playthrough.system: The fence opening persists. Footprints, sightlines and nearby infected make the risk legible without a surprise teleport.

playthrough.player: Spend scrap at the fixed barricade socket. See and hear it become stronger.
playthrough.system: Consume 3 scrap for the first repair; offer a second visible reinforcement for another 3. Four non-stacking slots make two trips useful without forcing an arbitrary delivery count.

playthrough.beat: A second trip with a reason
playthrough.player: Choose another 3 scrap for reinforcement, cloth against wounds, or food for stamina. The second trip offers preparation benefits rather than unlocking a hidden mandatory phase.
playthrough.system: Reuse the same interior with a different needed resource. Do not silently refill depleted containers.

playthrough.player: Return, inspect the street and choose when to begin the night sequence.
playthrough.system: Night becomes available after the first barricade repair. The intended two-trip rhythm is encouraged by the second reinforcement, not enforced. Dusk changes lighting and sound; do not punish slow first-time readers with an unavoidable timer.

playthrough.beat: The route comes back to you
playthrough.player: Deal with infected approaching through the available paths. Block, evade or use the melee tool.
playthrough.system: Spawn out of sight at fixed boundary points, never behind the player in a cleared room. Their navigation follows actual open links.

playthrough.player: See a concise outcome explaining observable events. Decide whether to retry with another plan.
playthrough.system: In research sessions, ask for the player's causal explanation before any explanatory result text or discussion. Use only a neutral survived/died screen until the response is logged. Then show the event summary and an equally easy finish/retry choice.

systems.name: Interaction and inventory
systems.implementation: Use one interactable interface for loot, fence, workbench, barricade and night-start. Interactions validate range and available slot/resource before changing state. Repeated input cannot duplicate items.
systems.acceptance: Every interactable has a readable prompt; a full inventory gives feedback; rapid repeated input never duplicates or loses resources.

systems.name: Persistent route state
systems.implementation: Keep one explicit fenceOpen boolean. A route controller updates the visible obstacle and navigation connection from the same state. Additional route objects are post-sprint work.
systems.acceptance: Opening the fence visibly changes both player access and the infected path. Ten consecutive resets restore the same closed starting state.

systems.name: Infected behaviour
systems.implementation: States: idle, investigate, pursue, attack and recover/repath. A noise event supplies a position and intensity; the AI must not track an unseen player forever. Cap active agents at six and avoid dynamic mesh rebuilding.
systems.acceptance: Test the longest route, every doorway and both fence states. No permanent stuck agent, attack through a closed wall or damage before the attack cue.

systems.name: Night director
systems.implementation: Choose fixed spawn groups and approach targets according to actual route availability. Keep wave count and enemy attributes the same when comparing route choices so the effect is inspectable.
systems.acceptance: A closed shortcut reroutes enemies instead of merely reducing an unseen difficulty score. Both route choices can be survived by a prepared player.

systems.name: Crafting and wound cost
systems.implementation: Two data-driven recipes consume resources atomically. A bandage removes the single wound state. Barricade strength uses a small discrete range with clear intact/damaged/broken visuals.
systems.acceptance: Each repair costs 3 scrap, bandage 1 cloth. Never duplicate or destroy an item when a full inventory becomes wounded: drop at a tested reachable anchor. Test every slot occupied and both repair tiers.

systems.name: Session flow and measurement
systems.implementation: One explicit phase state machine owns transitions. Collect consented local event logs or a manual test sheet; an analytics backend is not a sprint dependency.
systems.acceptance: Escape pauses safely, death reaches an outcome, retry resets every route/loot flag, and every log includes a build version.

controls: WASD move; mouse look; E interact; 1–4 select a slot; one melee input. Keep crafting at the workbench with two explicit choices.
Ship sensitivity, volume and readable key prompts. Make camera bob optional, keep small text out of the core loop and avoid colour-only threat cues.
Pair the main noise cue with visible environmental feedback. Provide pause, restart and clear quit controls; do not trap a player in a failed run.
Lock a representative test PC on day one. Provisional target: stable 60 fps at 1080p on that machine; measure frame time and worst-case six-enemy encounters before stating system requirements.

capacity.assumption: 15 working days, not 15 calendar days. Two senior developers and one artist provide 45 maker-days; the PM and marketer provide 30 additional days for testing and communication, not programming. Estimates assume a familiar engine, reusable controller/rig and licensed assets.

roles.allocation: Movement/interaction 3; inventory/recipes 2; melee/wound 2; HUD/onboarding 2; instrumentation/build 1; integration and fixes 5.
Phase/route loop 3; navigation/infected 4; night director 2; outcome/reset 1; integration, performance and fixes 5.
Modular block/interiors 4; props 2; licensed rig integration 1; lighting/readability 3; feedback effects 1; capture/capsule assets 2; fixes 2.
Scope and acceptance criteria; daily playable checks; recruit/schedule testers; classify failures; source/asset licence check; Steam release checklist.
Audience/competitor notes; creator shortlist; honest capture; two hook cuts; store copy and attribution log; outreach preparation and post-test synthesis.

capacity.budget: Salary, contractor, asset and marketing costs are not supplied. Day one: insert actual internal day rates and permitted asset costs. Do not infer a full-game budget or expected profit from wishlists.
dependencies: A familiar, shippable controller and animation pipeline.
Rights to use every asset, animation, sound and font.
A stable Windows build process and one representative test machine.
Access to target testers and the actual Steamworks release checklist.
capacity.reserve: Ten of the 30 developer-days are reserved for integration, performance and fixes. If core work overruns, cut optional mechanics before spending this entire reserve.

roadmap.outcome: Define and block out the promise
roadmap.devA: Controller, interaction and four-slot inventory skeleton.
roadmap.devB: Street layout, phase skeleton, fence state and test enemy path.
roadmap.artist: Greybox plus one modular wall/door/fence kit.
roadmap.pm: Set success definitions, actual costs, test hardware and Steam eligibility.
roadmap.marketing: Map three direct comparables and recruit the first five relevant testers.
roadmap.gate: A player can walk both routes and see the home. No polished capsule before the loop exists.

roadmap.devA: Loot, return, one barricade recipe and outcome UI.
roadmap.devB: Fence-controlled path, one night group, death and retry.
roadmap.pm: Run complete loops daily; prioritize blockers over preferences.
roadmap.marketing: Capture internal evidence; ask what the core decision is.
roadmap.gate: One unassisted rough trip → repair → night → reset. If absent, remove wound/food temporarily and keep the fence.

roadmap.devA: Second trip, bandage, basic melee and onboarding feedback.
roadmap.devB: Noise investigation, route edge cases and night pacing.
roadmap.artist: Readable props, signs of danger, one coherent infected rig.
roadmap.pm: Five cold usability sessions with recorded confusion points.
roadmap.marketing: Two honest 15-second openings, same build and same core footage.
roadmap.gate: Proposed gate: four of five explain benefit and consequence. If not, revise cues/choice; do not add another street.

roadmap.devA: Settings, reliable UI and event logging.
roadmap.devB: Navigation matrix, deterministic reset and worst-case performance.
roadmap.artist: Lighting, attack cue, repair states and capture-ready angles.
roadmap.pm: Freeze an eligible near-final release candidate around day eight if aiming for a day-fifteen public demo. Otherwise keep public release separate from the sprint; review may require rework.
roadmap.marketing: Prepare store text, press kit and fifteen audience-matched creator candidates.
roadmap.gate: No second door in this candidate. Content freeze by day ten for the prototype; material changes to a submitted build may invalidate the release timing assumption.

roadmap.devA: Fix onboarding, interaction and crash issues.
roadmap.devB: Fix AI, phase transitions and performance.
roadmap.artist: Resolve clarity problems and inconsistent asset presentation.
roadmap.pm: Freeze a measurement build for fifteen fresh target players, separate from the day-seven five. Split results into distinct cohorts if a consequential fix changes onboarding, route logic or combat.
roadmap.marketing: Use separate fresh viewers for hook-cut comprehension; do not prime the uncoached gameplay cohort with the consequence clip before playing. Keep placement and denominator records.
roadmap.gate: Do not announce public availability while the build or review checklist is unready.

roadmap.outcome: Deliver a build and an honest story
roadmap.devA: Release candidate, packaging and regression pass.
roadmap.devB: Final complete-run/reset checks and technical handoff.
roadmap.artist: Final capture and public asset check.
roadmap.pm: Publish the decision memo: counts, failures, limitations and next scope.
roadmap.marketing: Release only the approved build; provide real footage and record coverage. Otherwise deliver a private test build and video.
roadmap.gate: Choose continue, revise or stop from the gates below—not from a viral impression target.

metrics.definition: Report two separate measures: fresh clip viewers who name both the choice’s benefit and later consequence / viewers tested; unprimed first-time players who explain their own consequence / first-time players tested.
metrics.collection: Ask gameplay participants before explanatory outcome text or researcher discussion. Code responses before revealing the intended mechanism. Do not pool clip and play cohorts.
metrics.decision: Usability signal, not a forecast of sales.

metrics.definition: First runs resolving the night—surviving or dying during it—/ consented first runs started in one build cohort. Also show survival, night deaths, pre-night deaths, quits and crashes separately.
metrics.collection: Keep crashes and quits visible. Do not remove difficult sessions to improve the ratio.
metrics.decision: Find onboarding and pacing failure; do not compare a 15-minute slice to a multi-hour roguelike median.

metrics.definition: Eligible first-run finishers who start an unprompted second run and play for at least two minutes / eligible finishers offered the same option.
metrics.collection: Do not pay an extra incentive for replay or count tester instructions as intent.
metrics.decision: Evidence for a second decision, not long-term retention.

metrics.definition: Relevant contacted creators, replies, actual played coverage and measured visits as separate counts.
metrics.collection: Record outlet, date, prior comparable coverage and paid/unpaid/unknown status.
metrics.decision: A view count does not identify unique viewers or attributable wishlists.

metrics.definition: Retain Steamworks' own tracked/trusted-visit and conversion definitions, time windows and privacy restrictions.
metrics.collection: Use a consistent UTM source/medium/campaign convention if the store page is ready. Keep overall gross additions/removals/net stock separate.
metrics.decision: Unknown attribution stays unknown; no universal wishlist-to-sales multiplier.

instrumentation: Use a random session identifier, build ID, elapsed seconds, phase, route state and run index. Store minimal consented logs; do not record names, voice or unnecessary account identifiers. Test consent-off behaviour. Source cohort can be a recruitment code, not personal identity.

gates.pass: One complete rough loop and clean reset.
gates.revise: Cut wound/food and optional interactions until the route choice works.
gates.stop: If the team cannot implement the core route consequence in the familiar stack, pivot the prototype rather than promise a larger world.

gates.pass: Proposed usability gate: at least 4 of 5 fresh testers explain the benefit and later cost without being told.
gates.revise: Change cues, alternatives or encounter layout; rerun with fresh testers.
gates.stop: Do not interpret pretty screenshots as validation if the choice remains unreadable.

gates.pass: Proposed directional gate on one measurement build: 15 fresh target-player starts; at least 10 resolve the night (survive or die during it), at least 10 explain the route consequence before debrief, and at least 5 eligible finishers voluntarily replay for 2+ minutes. Report completion as X/15 and replay as Y/eligible finishers.
gates.revise: A cohort with fewer than 15 starts is incomplete, not an automatically relaxed gate. Preserve all failures. Split materially changed builds, and keep the five day-seven testers out of the fifteen-player cohort.
gates.stop: If the promise is understood but target players do not want another run, pause expansion and revise the core experience.

gates.pass: No known progress-blocking bugs in the final repeated-run checklist; approved store/build and release eligibility confirmed in Steamworks.
gates.revise: Deliver the playable test build plus accurately labeled video while fixing or awaiting review.
gates.stop: Never mark a video, unreviewed build or planned demo as a live Steam demo.

gateCaveat: All thresholds above are predeclared editorial decisions for this prototype, not Steam benchmarks or statistically powered evidence of market demand. Fifteen recruited players are a biased, small sample. Passing supports another experiment, not a production greenlight by itself.

marketing.deliverable: One-sentence promise, three competitor differences, a log of player problems to test.
marketing.avoid: Do not claim 'the first FPS Zomboid' or a proven gap.

marketing.deliverable: 0–4s: open the shortcut and save effort. 4–9s: night arrives and infected use that gap. 9–15s: the player responds and the consequence is clear.
marketing.avoid: Do not stage an unavailable mechanic or disguise a cinematic as gameplay.

marketing.deliverable: Short description, unedited run, accurate screenshots, controls, build limitations and access instructions. Select fifteen creators from recent comparable coverage.
marketing.avoid: Audience fit beats an arbitrary follower minimum; no paid commitments without a budget.

marketing.action: Run a small, trackable release test
marketing.deliverable: If stable and eligible, contact the first five suitable creators, collect actual coverage and expand only as support capacity allows. Compare hook cuts within a channel before comparing platforms.
marketing.avoid: Do not add YouTube, Twitch and TikTok views as unique reach or attribute every wishlist spike to outreach.

marketing.action: Publish what the test taught us
marketing.deliverable: Share the result and next change; retain or revise the promise according to the test. Share a real player-created incident only with permission.
marketing.avoid: No repeated demand for wishlists without a new reason to care.

risks.response: Prove both routes by day four, use fixed navigation and capped agents.
risks.cut: Remove optional path changes before replacing the navigation system.

risks.response: Use the exact route state, fair cues and identical enemy capability in comparison runs.
risks.cut: Simplify the encounter until players can attribute the result to their own choice.

risks.response: Reuse a proven controller/rig and give artist time to attack/readability cues.
risks.cut: Remove firearms, physics doors and elaborate hand interactions.

risks.risk: Co-op demand masks a solo mismatch
risks.response: Record play-mode preference and describe the actual demo before asking for interest.
risks.cut: Do not add networking mid-sprint; treat it as a separate feasibility decision.

risks.response: Check the account and app checklist on day one, submit with buffer and keep a private-build fallback.
risks.cut: Do not promise a festival slot or public release before approval.

risks.risk: Small test looks stronger than it is
risks.response: Retain raw counts, recruitment source, build version and adverse results.
risks.cut: No revenue forecast from fifteen testers or a few clips.

nextSteps.decision: Spend a short, explicitly budgeted repair iteration on the current block. Do not grow the world.
Change the player's central decision or audience promise. Test again before producing more environments.
Run a fresh cohort and a separate price/expectation conversation. Estimate actual full-game costs and support requirements.

Only after repeated evidence, consider a 6–8-week vertical slice with a second connected street and persistent refuge progression. A second route object can be tested here. Multiplayer and world simulation require separate estimates.

distribution.committedDeliverable: By day fifteen: a stable labeled prototype, an unedited run, a short honest clip and a decision memo. Public Steam demo is conditional on actual eligibility and review.
distribution.candidate: If targeting a day-fifteen public demo, freeze and submit eligible near-final materials around day eight with the base page ready. Do not assume 7-business-day planning allowance is a guaranteed approval time.

constraints.claim: Steam onboarding lists a 30-day interval between paying the app fee and releasing a game for a partner's first few titles.
constraints.definition: Game-release eligibility measured from fee payment, not 30 development workdays.
constraints.caveat: The docs phrase this for the first few titles, not every app forever. The provided sources do not explicitly resolve a new partner's demo eligibility under this interval; verify the actual Steamworks checklist or ask Steam support before promising a date.
constraints.planningImplication: A new full-game release cannot be promised inside a three-calendar-week sprint if this wait starts on day one.

constraints.claim: The full game's public Coming Soon page must be visible for at least two weeks before its release.
constraints.definition: A public store-presence interval, separate from fee payment and review time.
constraints.caveat: Do not add 30 days and 14 days automatically; requirements can overlap. Do not transfer this rule to a demo's own optional upcoming page.

constraints.claim: Store-page and product-build review each typically take 3–5 business days; Valve asks for at least 7 business days of planning allowance for each.
constraints.definition: Typical review duration and recommended buffer, not a guaranteed service deadline.
constraints.caveat: Submit a near-final build. Rework may be required. The dedicated Review Process page specifies business days; it is more precise than the shorter onboarding summary.
constraints.planningImplication: For a day-15 Steam demo target, plan the near-final candidate and store preparation early, not on day 15. Day 8 is a proposed latest candidate target, not a Valve guarantee.

constraints.claim: A demo has a separate App ID linked to its base game, its own configuration and review checklist. Before a pre-release demo goes live, the base game's store page must be public as Coming Soon.
constraints.definition: A Steam demo is not releasing the commercial base app.
constraints.caveat: The demo's own upcoming phase is explicitly optional: a fully reviewed demo can release directly to playable. This is not evidence that all new-partner onboarding constraints are waived.

constraints.claim: After the first playable demo release, its owner can trigger one wishlist notification to base-game wishlisters within the first two weeks.
constraints.definition: An optional once-only action, not automatic notification on every update.
constraints.caveat: The documentation also describes a two-week wishlist-notification cooldown. An early rough public demo can consume a useful launch moment; a private prototype handoff is a separate deliverable.

constraints.claim: Review checks require store screenshots to show gameplay and listed supported features to exist in the current build; future content must be clearly distinguished.
constraints.definition: Product representation rules, not evidence that a prototype will pass review.
constraints.caveat: Label one-street prototype footage honestly. Do not present a mockup, cinematic or unbuilt open world as shipped gameplay.

constraints.claim: UTM Total Visits count visits with tagged URLs. Trusted Visits exclude bots/crawlers. Tracked Visits are signed-in visits with abnormal repeated traffic excluded.
constraints.definition: Visits, not unique people or impressions.
constraints.caveat: Report these denominators separately. Small campaign rows may be hidden by privacy thresholds; absence of a row is not zero demand.

constraints.claim: Steam attributes wishlists, purchases and free-game/key activations to tracked UTM visits when the action occurs within 72 hours of the click.
constraints.definition: Attributed store action within a fixed window, not proof that the link caused the action.
constraints.caveat: Browser, device and app transitions can break attribution, although Steam's supported open-in-client/app banners can preserve it. UTM Analytics does not measure demo completion, route comprehension or voluntary replay; collect those separately with consent.
